title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated deepfake content was used to fabricate a news article featuring two real, named public figures. The article depicted a confrontation that never happened and was designed to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The failure is not a malfunction of a legitimate system but a deliberate misuse of AI tools to produce convincing false material at scale, outside any regulated deployment context.

The broader pattern identified by ASIC shows that this kind of fraud operates across several layers: fake websites, fabricated news articles, and scripted follow-up contact with potential investors. Each layer is designed to pass a casual credibility check, and the combination makes it harder for an ordinary person to identify any single element as fraudulent. Catching it would require either platform-level detection of synthetically generated media before publication or active verification by the audience against official financial registers, neither of which is a reliable front-line defence at present.

What is not established: ASIC's warning and the reported removal of scam content are regulatory actions and public advisories, not court findings, and no determination of individual criminal liability appears in the reporting.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake news article featuring Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler never actually occurred, but it was designed to promote Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated story described a heated confrontation between the two over the platform, which the government warns people to avoid. This incident exemplifies a growing type of scam that uses artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfake content featuring well-known Australians.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that investment scams using AI-generated deepfakes are rapidly increasing in sophistication. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams, up 182 percent, including 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, and finance presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC advises people to verify financial licenses through official registers and warns that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy. Scammers typically build elaborate fake websites, news articles, and advertisements before contacting potential investors with scripted calls and false investment opportunities.
